title: Angkor
hookLine: Jayavarman VII, a Buddhist king of Cambodia, and the smiling faces of the Bayon

cards: Climb the steep stone steps of the Bayon, at the heart of the old city of Angkor Thom in Cambodia, and the faces find you before you find them.
A great stone face on a tower, eyes half closed, lips turned up at the corners. Turn your head, and there's another, looking off in a different direction. Then another, on the next tower over.
Moss in the cracks, lichen on the cheeks, and still that same calm, closed-mouth smile. Visitors have argued for a long time about whose face it is.

teach.h: JAYAVARMAN VII, A BUDDHIST KING AT ANGKOR.
teach.b: First, the king. Angkor was the seat of a great Khmer kingdom, and kings there had built huge temples, some of them for Hindu gods, like Vishnu at Angkor Wat.
King Jayavarman the Seventh was a Buddhist, of the Mahayana stream, and when he built his walled city he put the Bayon at its center.

teach.h: WHOSE FACES? NOBODY CAN SAY FOR SURE.
teach.b: Second, the question nobody can settle. The temple left no label on the faces. Some scholars see the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, called Lokeshvara in Cambodia.
Some see the king himself. Some see both at once: a ruler who wanted to be seen as compassion turned in every direction. The honest answer: nobody knows, and the stone doesn't say.
Third, the bodhisattva behind the guess.

In the Lotus Sutra, Avalokiteshvara is the one who hears beings who call out in trouble and comes to help, taking whatever form will reach them. A face turned to every point of the compass fits that picture well.
Fourth, what the king's own words add.
Inscriptions from his reign tell of hospitals and rest houses he founded, and one hospital inscription says, in substance, that the suffering of his people was his own pain.
A king can say beautiful things, and historians weigh them carefully.
But it is the same idea as the towers: a face that doesn't look away. And the smile itself? It isn't laughing at anything, or grinning for a camera.
It has nowhere in particular to point: gentle, a little inward, offered to whoever happens to be standing there.

how: Cambodian Buddhists and visitors from many places come to the Bayon at Angkor Thom, and in Mahayana Buddhism Avalokiteshvara is honored as the bodhisattva of compassion, often called on in chant and prayer.

games.q: you're standing on the upper terrace of the Bayon, and a friend asks whose face is on the towers. what's the honest answer?
o: it's the king, and the stone says so.
it's the bodhisattva, and nobody disputes it.
nobody knows for sure; Lokeshvara, the king, or both.
games.why: the stone carries no label. scholars have proposed Lokeshvara, the king, and a blend of the two, and the question is still open.

practice: Let your eyes half close like the faces on the towers, and let the corners of your mouth lift just slightly, not a grin, not for anyone.
Breathe in and out with the small smile, noticing the eyes, the jaw, the shoulders, and if it fades or feels strange, let it return without fuss.

wordCard.voice: Angkor. The old Khmer capital in Cambodia, where King Jayavarman the Seventh raised the Bayon and its towers of quiet, smiling faces. Today's word.
